posts.copy:
China made 18.9% more industrial robots in September 2026 than a year earlier. It made 17.8% fewer service robots.

Both numbers sit in the same official release, two rows apart.

Read from a desk in London or New York, the China robot story is humanoids doing backflips. That is the part that films well. It is not the part that is compounding.

The National Bureau of Statistics counted 96,752 industrial robots made in September alone, and 794,781 across the first nine months of the year, up 29.1%.

The machines that build things kept growing. The service robots, the category closest to the consumer, went backwards in the month.

On the ground, that demand is not in the showroom. It is in the integrators fitting arms onto lines that already exist, and in factory managers who talk about payback periods rather than demos.

The signal is rarely in the product that trends. It is usually in the dull row of the table that keeps growing.

If you want to see this on the ground for yourself, work with us.

DM us, or write to us at hello@oj.ventures

Source: National Bureau of Statistics of China, 20 October 2026: https://www.stats.gov.cn/english/PressRelease/202610/t20261020_1965665.html?utm_source=linkedin&utm_medium=organic&utm_campaign=A-OJV202647-M

posts.copy:
In 2005 a Chinese PC maker put its executive headquarters in Purchase, New York. Not by accident, but by design.

Lenovo did not need to learn how to build a computer. What it did not have was the Western buyer.

Enterprise IT buys from a name it already trusts, through a rep it already knows, with financing and service it already has contracts for.

So Lenovo bought IBM's PC business, in a deal completed on 1 May 2005, for US$1.25 billion: about US$650 million in cash and US$600 million in Lenovo shares.

Lenovo's PCs would be marketed through IBM's worldwide distribution and sales network. IBM became its preferred supplier of services and financing. IBM ended up owning 18.9% of Lenovo, so the old seller had a reason to keep selling.

The buyer, the financing and the story came in one deal, not built from zero.

Most Asian companies moving West spend year one proving the product. The product is rarely what is missing. The buyer is a different person, and the story has to land in a room that never saw your home-market win.

You do not need a billion dollars to apply this. You need to know which relationship your buyer already trusts, and route through it. That is the first thing our GTM advisory work maps.

We were not involved in Lenovo's deal. This is commentary.

If you want your move into the West to look like this, work with us.

DM us, or write to us at hello@oj.ventures

posts.copy:
Give us an hour with an Asian company moving into the West and we can usually tell which home habit will cost it the first year.

We start with four things:

→ Who signs
→ What they compare you to
→ Price
→ Proof

Then we look at what is underneath them.

Is the person who signs in Germany or Texas the same role that signed at home, or has the budget moved to someone you have never pitched?

When a Western buyer shortlists you, which incumbent are you compared to, and does your deck know its name?

Was your price rebuilt for how that buyer's procurement works, or converted from your home currency?

Is your proof a logo they recognise, or a home-market win they have to take on trust?

From the inside this usually looks like a brand problem. Nobody has heard of us, so the answer must be more marketing. Sometimes it is. More often the product is fine and the buyer, the pricing and the story were never rebuilt for the new room.

APAC is not one market, it is 15+ ecosystems, and the West is not one market either. The job is rapid recalibration, not a rigid playbook.

If you are an Asian company taking a proven product into Western markets and the first meetings are not converting, work with us.

DM us, or write to us at hello@oj.ventures
